title: Motifs et théorie de Hodge : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Grothendieck is setting up Hodge-theoretic structures on algebraic de Rham cohomology H*(X) = H*(X, Ω•_X), which he calls 'cohomologie de Hodge', for X smooth projective over a field K that carries a topology.

Previous page. For K a topological field isomorphic to C, a topological isomorphism u: K → C gives a comparison H*(X_top, K) ≅ H*(X) and a Hodge decomposition φ. Neither depends on u. The only continuous automorphisms of C are the identity and complex conjugation c, and changing u by c is absorbed by the semilinear extension of c to the coefficients.

This page. Now let K be (abstractly) isomorphic to R. He remarks that one need not fix an identification, because R has no nontrivial automorphisms. Let K' be an algebraic closure (≅ C) and π = Gal(K'/K) = Z/2. Applying the C-case to X_{K'} gives
 φ_{K'}: ⊕_{p,q} H^q(X, Ω^p) ⊗_K K' ≅ H*(X) ⊗_K K'.
By the independence of u shown before, φ_{K'} commutes with the semilinear π-action. Hence by Galois descent it comes from a K-isomorphism
 φ: ⊕_{p,q} H^q(X, Ω^p_X) ≅ H*(X).
In modern terms: for X smooth projective over R, the Hodge decomposition of H_dR(X/R) ⊗ C is stable under the de Rham conjugation id ⊗ c. Under the comparison isomorphism this conjugation corresponds to F_∞ ∘ c_B. Both F_∞ and c_B swap H^{p,q} and H^{q,p}, so the composite preserves each H^{p,q}. The H^{p,q} are therefore defined over R inside H_dR(X/R).

Summary claim. Over any 'locally compact non-discrete' (in practice archimedean) topological field one gets a canonical decomposition φ, compatible with the Hodge filtration. He sets H^{p,q}(X) = φ(H^q(X, Ω^p)) ⊂ F^p.

Last lines and next page. For K without a topology (e.g. a number field), choosing an archimedean topology T gives a decomposition φ_T after completing. One then intersects back with H*(X) to get K-subspaces H^{p,q}_T(X). Their 'real' versions are vector spaces over R_T, and after intersecting over all T, over the maximal totally real subfield K_r.

Margin. There is a canonical R-isomorphism H*(X(C), R) ⊗_R C ≅ H*(X) ⊗_R C. It is compatible with π acting both on X(C) and on the coefficients C. Taking invariants gives:
- H*(X)^+ ≅ H*(X(C), R)^π = H*(X(C)/π, R), with X_top = X(C)/F_∞;
- H*(X) = H*(X)^+ ⊕ H*(X)^-, with H*(X)^- matching the (−1)-eigenspace H_B^- (up to a factor i).
In modern language: H_dR(X/R) ≅ (H_B ⊗ C)^{F_∞ ⊗ c} = H_B^+ ⊕ i·H_B^-. This is exactly the decomposition underlying Deligne's periods c^±.
errors: The summary 'corps top. localement (quasi-)compact non discret' as stated would include p-adic and Laurent-series fields, where no such Hodge decomposition exists. The argument only works for archimedean (connected) locally compact fields, i.e. R and C, as the next page's restriction to completions ≅ R or C confirms.
Boxed formula: H^{p,q} should sit in F^p H^{p+q}(X), not F^p H^q(X), unless an unusual indexing is intended.
Margin: H*(X)^- corresponds to i·H_B^- (the −1 eigenspace twisted by i), not literally H_B^-, if one wants a real-structure-compatible identification. This is minor and probably intended.
The identification H(X(C), R)^π = H(X(C)/π, R) holds with real (or rational) coefficients via transfer. That is fine, but it fails integrally, which is not noted.

ideas.what: Hodge decomposition of de Rham cohomology is canonical for a topological field ≅ C and descends via Galois to fields ≅ R; the H^{p,q} are defined over R for X over R
ideas.modern_name: Real Hodge structure on H_dR(X/R) with de Rham conjugation F_∞∘c_B; Hodge decomposition defined over R
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; made systematic by Deligne (Valeurs de fonctions L et périodes d'intégrales, 1979; Hodge II/III)

ideas.what: Decomposition H_dR(X/R) ≅ H_B^+ ⊕ (i)H_B^- with H_B^+ = H(X(C)/F_∞, R)
ideas.modern_name: F_∞-eigenspace decomposition of Betti cohomology; real Deligne/Beilinson setup; periods c^±

ideas.what: For K a field with several archimedean topologies T, define K-rational parts H^{p,q}_T(X) = φ_T(...) ∩ H*(X) and real versions over R_T, then over the maximal totally real subfield K_r
ideas.modern_name: Rationality of Hodge decomposition at infinite places; Hodge structures of motives over number fields / absolute Hodge setups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Hodge cycles on abelian varieties, 1982; 1979 periods paper)

missed.claim: Grothendieck (c. 1969–72) already records the splitting of real de Rham cohomology into Betti F_∞-invariant and anti-invariant parts, interpreting the invariant part as the cohomology of the quotient X(C)/complex conjugation. This is the structure behind Deligne's c^± periods (1979) and Beilinson's real Deligne cohomology.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority only. It shows the + / − real structures entered Grothendieck's motivic Hodge notes years before Deligne's period conjecture, though as a routine observation.

missed.claim: Program to attach to each archimedean topology T of an abstract field K a K-rational (or K_r-rational) Hodge piece H^{p,q}_T ∩ H*(X), and to intersect over all T. The page only sets this up and stops.
missed.quote: Si K n'est pas topologique, ... choix d'une topologie ... T sur K, on déduit une
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is close to studying the Hodge decompositions at all complex embeddings simultaneously (absolute Hodge / Hodge structures of motives over number fields). That is well developed now, so the novelty is low.

deep.surprise_reason: Mathematically standard (descent of Hodge decomposition to R, F_∞ eigenspaces), but an early unpublished Grothendieck formulation of the H^+ / H^- real structure later central to Deligne's periods. Mild historical interest.
transcription_corrections: 'top. loc. quasi compact [?] non discret' is probably 'top. loc. compact non discret' (the restriction to archimedean is implicit).
Boxed inclusion likely reads F^p H^{p+q}(X) in intent, though the hand seems to write F^pH^q(X).
The margin's first line reads 'On a aussi un R-isomorphisme canonique (π = Z/2Z) H*(X_{C top}, R) ⊗_R C ≅ H*(X) ⊗_R C, qui est compatible avec π opérant sur X_C et π opérant sur C dans ⊗_R C'.
